keyConcepts.title: Process-to-process delivery
keyConcepts.text: The network layer delivers between **hosts**. The transport layer extends that to **processes**, using port numbers (multiplexing and demultiplexing).

keyConcepts.title: Demultiplexing: UDP vs. TCP
keyConcepts.text: A UDP socket is identified by a **2-tuple** (destination IP, destination port). A TCP socket is identified by a **4-tuple** (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port).

keyConcepts.title: UDP
keyConcepts.text: Connectionless, no handshake, no connection state and an 8-byte header with a checksum. Used when speed and control matter more than reliability (DNS, real-time apps, QUIC).

keyConcepts.title: Building reliability (rdt)
keyConcepts.text: Checksums detect errors, ACKs/NAKs give feedback, sequence numbers catch duplicates, and timers recover from loss. rdt3.0 (alternating-bit) works, but stop-and-wait is slow.

keyConcepts.title: Pipelining: GBN vs. SR
keyConcepts.text: Go-Back-N uses cumulative ACKs and one timer, and resends everything on timeout. Selective Repeat ACKs each packet, buffers out-of-order packets and resends only lost ones (window ≤ half the sequence space).

keyConcepts.title: TCP reliability
keyConcepts.text: Byte-stream sequence numbers, cumulative ACKs, one retransmission timer, **TimeoutInterval = EstimatedRTT + 4·DevRTT**, and **fast retransmit** after 3 duplicate ACKs.

keyConcepts.title: Flow control
keyConcepts.text: The receiver advertises **rwnd** (free buffer space), and the sender keeps unacknowledged data ≤ rwnd so it doesn't overflow the receiver.

keyConcepts.title: Connection management
keyConcepts.text: Three-way handshake: **SYN, SYNACK, ACK**. Teardown uses FIN segments and a TIME_WAIT state. SYN cookies defend against SYN floods.

keyConcepts.title: Congestion control (AIMD)
keyConcepts.text: **Slow start** doubles cwnd each RTT up to ssthresh, **congestion avoidance** adds 1 MSS per RTT, and loss halves cwnd (3 duplicate ACKs) or resets it to 1 MSS (timeout).

keyConcepts.title: Modern congestion control and QUIC
keyConcepts.text: CUBIC (Linux default), delay-based BBR and ECN marking. QUIC runs over UDP with a combined secure handshake and independent streams.

flashcards.back: Transport: logical communication between processes. Network: logical communication between hosts.
Delivering the data in an arriving segment to the correct socket, using port numbers.
A 2-tuple: (destination IP address, destination port number).
A 4-tuple: (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port).
8 bytes: source port, destination port, length and checksum (2 bytes each).
No connection setup delay, no connection state, a smaller header, and the app controls exactly when data is sent.
Add 16-bit words with one's-complement wraparound and flip the bits. The receiver adds everything including the checksum; all 1s means no error detected.
Error detection, receiver feedback (ACK/NAK) and retransmission.
Garbled ACKs/NAKs, by adding sequence numbers so the receiver can detect duplicate packets.
A countdown timer, so the sender retransmits when a packet or ACK is lost.
**U = (L/R) / (RTT + L/R)**, which is tiny on fast, long links.
Resend ALL unacknowledged packets in the window. The receiver discards out-of-order packets.
Window size must be ≤ half the sequence number space, or the receiver can't tell new packets from retransmissions.
MSS: max application data in a TCP segment (often 1460 bytes). MTU: max link-layer frame payload (1500 bytes for Ethernet).
The byte-stream number of the first byte in the segment.
The sequence number of the next byte the receiver expects (cumulative ACK).
**EstimatedRTT = (1 − α)·EstimatedRTT + α·SampleRTT**, with α = 0.125.
**EstimatedRTT + 4·DevRTT**, where DevRTT = (1 − β)·DevRTT + β·|SampleRTT − EstimatedRTT| and β = 0.25.
After 3 duplicate ACKs, resend the missing segment right away instead of waiting for the timer.
rwnd = RcvBuffer − (LastByteRcvd − LastByteRead). The sender keeps LastByteSent − LastByteAcked ≤ rwnd.
SYN (client_isn) → SYNACK (server_isn, ACK client_isn + 1) → ACK (may carry data).
SYN cookies: the server doesn't allocate state until it gets a valid ACK whose number matches a hash-based cookie.
cwnd starts at 1 MSS and grows by 1 MSS per ACK, which doubles it every RTT until it reaches ssthresh or a loss occurs.
After cwnd reaches ssthresh, it grows by about 1 MSS per RTT (linear).
ssthresh = cwnd/2, cwnd = 1 MSS, and back to slow start.

flashcards.front: TCP Reno reaction to 3 duplicate ACKs
flashcards.back: ssthresh = cwnd/2, cwnd = ssthresh + 3 MSS, then fast recovery.
Additive increase, multiplicative decrease: +1 MSS per RTT, halve on loss. It produces the sawtooth graph and converges to fairness.
About **0.75·W/RTT**, where W is the window size when loss occurs.
Explicit Congestion Notification: routers mark the IP header, the receiver sets ECE in its ACK, and the sender cuts cwnd and sets CWR.
A secure, reliable, congestion-controlled protocol built on UDP. It has one combined handshake and independent streams (no HOL blocking), and HTTP/3 uses it.

quiz.q: Two TCP segments arrive at a server with the same destination port but different source IP addresses. What happens?
options: They go to the same socket
quiz.explain: TCP sockets are identified by the full 4-tuple, so different sources mean different sockets.

quiz.q: Which field does UDP NOT have?
quiz.explain: UDP's 8-byte header has only source port, destination port, length and checksum. It has no sequence numbers.

quiz.q: What does adding sequence numbers in rdt2.1 solve?
options: Detecting duplicate packets caused by garbled ACKs/NAKs
quiz.explain: If the sender retransmits after a garbled ACK, the receiver uses the sequence number to tell it's a duplicate.

quiz.q: RTT = 30 ms, R = 1 Gbps, L = 8,000 bits. About what is stop-and-wait sender utilization?
quiz.explain: L/R = 0.008 ms, so U = 0.008 / 30.008 ≈ 0.00027. The sender is busy only 0.027% of the time.

quiz.q: In Go-Back-N, what does the receiver do with an out-of-order packet?
options: Discards it and re-ACKs the last in-order packet
Buffers it and ACKs it individually
quiz.explain: The GBN receiver keeps it simple: it only accepts in-order packets.

quiz.q: Why must Selective Repeat's window be at most half the sequence number space?
options: So the receiver can tell new packets from retransmissions of old ones
To make the timer more accurate
quiz.explain: With too large a window, an old retransmitted packet and a new packet can carry the same sequence number, and the receiver can't tell them apart.

quiz.q: A host has received bytes 0–999 from the other side. What acknowledgment number does it send?
quiz.explain: The ACK number is the next byte expected.

quiz.q: When does a TCP sender do a fast retransmit?
quiz.explain: Three duplicate ACKs strongly suggest the next segment was lost, so it's resent before the timer expires.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of TCP flow control?
options: Prevent the sender from overflowing the receiver's buffer
quiz.explain: Flow control matches the sender's rate to how fast the receiving app reads data. Congestion control is about the network.

quiz.q: What is the correct order of the TCP three-way handshake?
quiz.explain: The client sends SYN, the server replies SYNACK, and the client sends ACK (which can carry data).

quiz.q: During slow start, how does cwnd grow?
options: It grows by 1 MSS per RTT
quiz.explain: cwnd grows by 1 MSS for each ACK, which doubles it each RTT (exponential growth).

quiz.q: cwnd = 16 MSS when a timeout occurs. What are ssthresh and cwnd afterward?
quiz.explain: On a timeout, ssthresh = cwnd/2 = 8 and cwnd resets to 1 MSS (slow start).
TCP adds 1 MSS per RTT and halves cwnd on loss, which gives the sawtooth pattern.

quiz.q: Why does QUIC avoid head-of-line blocking between streams?
options: Each stream is delivered reliably and in order on its own, so a loss only stalls its own stream
It sends everything in one packet
quiz.explain: QUIC multiplexes independent streams over UDP, so one lost packet doesn't block the others.

quiz.q: Which TCP version is the default in Linux?
quiz.explain: CUBIC grows cwnd as a cubic function of time since the last loss, quickly when far from W_max and carefully near it.
